lesson.title: One Element, Two Fates: Understanding Disproportionation
lesson.summary: Disproportionation is a special redox reaction in which a single element simultaneously undergoes both oxidation and reduction, splitting from one starting oxidation state into two different product oxidation states in the same reaction.
lesson.body:
In an ordinary redox reaction, one substance is oxidized while a completely different substance is reduced, as with zinc losing electrons to hydrogen ions in the previous chapter. Disproportionation is a special, almost self-contradictory case where a single element does both jobs at once: starting from one oxidation state, it ends up simultaneously at a higher oxidation state, oxidized, and a lower oxidation state, reduced, in the different products of the very same reaction. Spotting disproportionation requires exactly the skill built in assigning oxidation numbers, since you have to carefully track the same element's oxidation state on both sides of the equation and notice that it splits into two different values rather than staying the same or moving uniformly in one direction.

A classic real example is the instability of aqueous copper(I) ion. Copper(I), Cu+, is not very stable in water and disproportionates according to 2 Cu+(aq) to Cu(s) + Cu2+(aq). Assigning oxidation numbers, copper starts at positive 1 in both Cu+ ions on the left. On the right, one copper atom ends up as solid copper metal at an oxidation state of 0, while the other ends up as Cu2+ at positive 2. One copper(I) ion gained a single electron to become copper metal, so it was reduced, while the other copper(I) ion lost a single electron to become copper(II), so it was oxidized. The electron gained by one copper ion is exactly the electron lost by the other, and the overall charge balances too: positive 2 total on the left from two Cu+ ions, and 0 plus positive 2 on the right, also positive 2.

A second real, industrially important example is how household bleach is manufactured: chlorine gas dissolved in cold, dilute sodium hydroxide disproportionates according to Cl2(g) + 2 OH-(aq) to Cl-(aq) + OCl-(aq) + H2O(l). Chlorine starts at an oxidation state of 0 in Cl2 and ends up at negative 1 in chloride ion, reduced, and at positive 1 in hypochlorite ion, oxidized, both formed in the same reaction vessel from the same starting chlorine atoms.

Here is a worked numeric example, continuing the copper(I) case. Suppose a solution contains 0.0200 mol of Cu+ and it disproportionates completely. The balanced equation's 2 to 1 to 1 ratio between Cu+, Cu(s), and Cu2+ means exactly half of the starting copper ends up as solid metal and half ends up as Cu2+ remaining in solution. Moles of Cu(s) formed equal 0.0200 mol Cu+ times the ratio 1 mol Cu per 2 mol Cu+, which is 0.0100 mol. Using copper's molar mass of 63.55 g/mol, the mass of copper metal deposited is 0.0100 mol times 63.55 g/mol, which equals 0.636 g. By the same 1 to 2 ratio, 0.0100 mol of Cu2+ also remains dissolved in the solution.

Disproportionation shows up throughout the redox chemistry of elements that have several accessible intermediate oxidation states, and recognizing it is really just a matter of applying the oxidation-number bookkeeping you already know, carefully, to every atom of the same element on both sides of the equation.
